title: Faking, reading music, and playing by ear
summary: Hug explains 'fake', New Orleans non-readers, the stigma of not reading, and creativity from the ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I just wanted to ask you one thing about what you said. You said something earlier, very early in the discussion about a person you knew that played fake. Was that a term that was used, or still used?

Yeah, fake, yeah, fake was always a term that we used, because most of the New Orleans musicians were non-readers. You know, I mean, as Dick Allen knows, the old-time musicians like Papa Lane and, well, Shawky wasn't much of a reader.
Was there any stigma attached to that, the fact that you didn't read it, was that bad?

Well, if you want to know what it has, my first big job, as I told you, was the Foyant Dance Hall. Mm-hmm. Well, when I went there, I had some music that I used to carry around with me, you know, some sheet music and some of the popular tunes of that day, like, Yes, That's My Baby, or something like that, you know. I would have tucked away just to brief myself on a little bit, you know, in case I need it. Well, when I walked in with this music on my arm, Von Gammon, the drummer, says, He says, What do you got there, kid? I said, I got some music. He said, What are you going to do with it? He says, We don't read, they don't read, they don't read music here, you know. And he says, If you take a look around, see how dark it is in here, he says, You could see the music to start off with. I said, Well, how am I going to learn? He says, We'll teach you the numbers. I said, I don't know tunes like Jasmine Blues and Panama, Panama and High Society and all the old traditional tunes, you know. I said, I don't know those tunes. He says, Don't worry about it. We'll teach them to you. And that's the way I learned them. We start off a tune that said, Well, we're going to play That's A Plenty or something, you know, to that order. I said, I don't know what Harry Shields would be calling out to, he'd be telling me what chords are coming next, you know. I wouldn't play the melodies. He said, Just play the chords. That's all. Don't worry about the melody. Just play the chords until you get to learn it. And very often, I'd be going through some tune with them and I'd hit a bad chord and Harry Shields had a wonderful ear, you know. Harry would say, No, no, that's the wrong change. Oh, my Lord, you're hitting a bad change there. That's not the change. And then he'd tell me what the right chord was, you see. Well, this is the way the New Orleans musicians in the old, those days believed in learning. They listened to one another play and that's the way they played. And they felt that if you read music, you weren't playing jazz as good as it could be played. And basically, they are right because you don't read jazz music and play it with the right feeling. In other words, their interpretation was to play it, you had to play it from your heart and play it from your mind, but not reading it from the notes. But of course, you can use music as a guide, you know, and then put your own feeling into it. Well, that's what came along later on. But the reason most of the New Orleans musicians didn't read was that one reason, because they felt that if you read music, you weren't a real good jazz musician. That to play good jazz, you had to play by ear. Just pick it up.
Do you feel that way about Biggs's music, that the kind of things he worked out there were worked out on an ear basis? I know you mentioned that you thought it was a great...
Oh, definitely. He worked it out, surely.
I think they couldn't have done if he knew how it was.
Surely. He worked it out of his head and out of his mind and his heart.

That's what they meant by...creativity has to come from within. I mean, you know, you just don't read that on music. You can play somebody else's ideas that are already written down. But, I mean, to bring out your own ideas, you have to create. You have to bring something else out. And that can't be done unless you bring it out yourself. And this, you might say, is playing by ear. Sure. That's what it basically amounts to.

Well, it's been pointed out, I think, in that book that just came out on Biggs, that a lot of solo passages he managed to create. And they only could have been created by someone who played by ear. Sure. Because he went off on a note, for instance, that a person who read, a well-trained red musician, would have thought it was a mistake and completely stopped the solo. Yeah. But Biggs managed to go on because he didn't have that reading novel. So it actually worked to his best.

And this is true of many of the people who have studied music. Like, I have people come up right now and tell me, you know, I'm playing something. And they say, how long did you study? I say, oh, I actually studied about six months. I said, six months? I studied ten years. I can't play anything, you know? They said, all I can do is when I got the notes there, you know, I can play it. But when they take the music away from me, I can't play it. Well, that's what the old musicians in New Orleans used to avoid. They didn't want to fall into that category of just being able to play from the music. They'd rather pick it up and say that they played it and learned it by ear rather than say they read it. Of course, it didn't work out too well when you had to go somewhere. Like, I'll never forget the time I went to work with Johnny Detroit, one of the old New Orleans trumpet players who was a very fine musician. He wasn't a great jazz man, but he was a very, very fine musician. And I went to work with him at Suburban Gardens, and they had a, that was a nightclub, and they had a terrific dance act. And the music was so complicated, I'd never seen anything so difficult in all my life. It was written in three sharps, four sharps, five sharps, all keys that were so foreign to me because, and playing jazz, you don't use those keys too much, you know? Well, I started trying to read this music. I couldn't, I read the first three or four bars and that was it. So Johnny Detroit came over to me and says, I didn't hear any piano. I said, well, there's a good reason. I said, I wasn't playing. And he turned to me and says, that's the trouble with you dance musicians. He says, when you get something to read, you can't play it. I says, well, I said, I have to agree with you, you're right. So he says, well, take it home and we'll shed it, see what happens. The very next act came up, didn't have any music. So he says, what are we going to do? We can't play it if you don't have music. I said, what number do they want? They said, who's sorry now? I said, who's sorry now? I said, I can play that. He says, can you play it? You know it? I said, yeah. I asked them for that key. They wanted it in. And I gave them an introduction and I started playing. And the dancers, they were just thrilled that I could play it behind them. So he says, well, I have to admit, he says, that the dance musicians have got some good points. So you see, the faking, or as we called it, faking, did have a real great part in music. I mean, and it's something that even to today, I guess the musicians are happiest, the ones that are still playing the old time music. If they're playing something, a carnival ball, and they've been reading music, they fold up the music and say, let's forget about it. Let's play. Let's just jam all fake. Let's say stuff
